title: Design brief, research and ideas

book.title: My Revision Notes: AQA A Level Design and Technology: Product Design

needs: Explain why a design process is usually cyclic, and put its stages in order.
Describe what a design brief contains.
Describe ways to research existing products, materials and users, and to gather inspiration.
Explain what a design specification is, when it's written and how it's used.
Describe ideas generation methods, including SCAMPER and Thinking Hats.

doNow.q: What does a design brief outline?
doNow.a: The needs and wants of a specific user or target market.
Any three: mind maps, SCAMPER, collaborative team designing, the 4x4 technique, Thinking Hats, discussing designs with a client.
The ability to resist stretching by pulling forces.
Demand by consumers for desirable features.

clues: I help a designer explore a style before any ideas are drawn.
I'm made of images chosen for their styles and colours.

bigPicture.question: How do designers get from a problem to good ideas?

chunks.label: The design process
chunks.summary: An organised way of designing and making, usually repeated as a cycle.

items.ask: How might a designer organise the work from a problem to a finished prototype?
items.text: Designers follow a design process, working through a series of stages from the problem to testing a prototype. A design process is an organised way to design a product and make its prototype. Its stages include investigation, specification, ideas, modelling and planning production.

image.alt: Design process

items.ask: Why might a designer go round the same stages more than once?
items.text: Ongoing improvement matters to a product's commercial success, so each round refines the design. A cyclic (iterative) process is a design process that repeats its stages instead of being linear. Test results or user feedback can send a project back to earlier decisions.

image.alt: Cyclic (iterative) process

items.ask: Does every project need the same amount of research, modelling and testing?
items.text: Each project needs a different depth of investigation, modelling and testing. A design process gives structure, but it shouldn't be treated as a rigid recipe.

image.alt: Not a fixed recipe

items.text: The stages, starting from the problem:
steps: Testing and evaluation, then round again

image.alt: Diagram of the design cycle: eight numbered stages round a ring, from problem or brief to testing and evaluation.

check.q: Why is the design process usually cyclic rather than linear?
check.a: Ongoing improvements matter to commercial success, so the stages are repeated.

check.q: Which stage of the design cycle comes straight after the specification?

chunks.label: Design brief
chunks.summary: Sets out the problem and the needs of the user or target market.

items.ask: Before designing anything, what would you need to know about who it's for?
items.text: You'd need their needs and wants, which a design brief sets out. A design brief is an outline of the problem and of what a specific user or target market needs and wants. It comes first in the design cycle, before investigation.

image.alt: A designer and a client at a workshop table, going over printed sheets for a new project.

items.ask: What should a brief describe first?
items.text: A description of the problem or need comes first, setting out the situation to be solved.

image.alt: The problem

items.ask: How could a brief help a designer picture the situation?
items.text: Images and details of the context, situation or problem help the designer picture it.

image.alt: Context

items.ask: Why mention products that are already on sale?
items.text: To show where existing products fall short, being inadequate or unsuitable for the need. Primary research later analyses their strengths and weaknesses.

image.alt: Existing products

items.ask: Who else should a brief tell the designer about?
items.text: The brief gives information about the client or user group the product is for.

image.alt: Client or user

items.ask: How much should a brief say about the product itself?
items.text: Only a basic description of the product and its key functions, plus the key areas to focus on for success. The detailed criteria come later, in the design specification.

check.q: What does a design brief outline?
check.a: The needs and wants of a specific user or target market.

check.q: Name two things a design brief contains.
check.a: Any two: the problem or need; images of the context; shortcomings of existing products; client or user information; a basic description and key functions; key areas for success.

chunks.label: Primary research
chunks.summary: First-hand analysis of existing products: strengths, weaknesses and what to improve.

items.ask: How could you find out what's good and bad about products already on sale?
items.text: Analyse them for strengths, weaknesses and areas to improve, by using them and taking them apart. Primary research is information you collect directly for your own project. Methods include questionnaires, focus groups, interviews and observation.

image.alt: Primary research

items.ask: What's the quickest way to find out how well a product does its job?
items.text: Use it yourself for the task it was designed for, to get first-hand knowledge of how well it works.

image.alt: Using the product

items.ask: How could you discover how a product is put together and made?
items.text: Take it apart, so you can assess its function, components, materials and manufacture. The aim is to learn useful design lessons, not to copy the product.

image.alt: A games controller taken apart, its plastic case, circuit parts and wires laid out flat.
image.credit: repaired by Dmitry G · CC BY-SA 3.0

items.ask: How can you tell whether a product is better or worse than its rivals?
items.text: Compare its function, components, materials and manufacture with those of equivalent products.

image.alt: Five electric kettles of different designs lined up on a workshop bench.

items.ask: How could you get views on a product from people other than yourself?
items.text: Use focus groups or questionnaires to seek objective views from other people. A focus group is a guided group discussion that can show shared views and disagreements. Members can sway each other, so treat the results as qualitative evidence.

image.alt: A small group around a workshop table with paper questionnaires and wooden product models.

items.ask: Apart from how it looks, what makes a product right for its users?
items.text: Ease of use and meeting consumer needs matter, so assess its ergonomic features and check key development criteria are met. Ergonomics uses information about people to improve comfort, safety, efficiency and control.

image.alt: Two hands gripping a smooth wooden handle.

items.ask: What else would a customer judge before buying?
items.text: How it looks and what it costs, so assess the product's aesthetics and cost.

image.alt: Aesthetics and cost

check.q: Why would a designer take an existing product apart?
check.a: To assess its function, components, materials and manufacture.

check.q: Name two ways of getting objective views on a product from other people.

chunks.label: Materials and other research
chunks.summary: Research into materials, people, trends, constraints, standards and wider factors.

items.ask: How can a designer be sure a material is right before choosing it?
items.text: Research materials, construction and finishes, so the choices made are appropriate. Useful findings are turned into material requirements for the design.

image.alt: Materials research

items.ask: What facts about a material might a designer need from a specialist?
items.text: Technical data such as its toughness and tensile strength, supplied by specialist researchers. A tensile test finds tensile strength by pulling a sample apart while measuring force and extension.

image.alt: A universal testing machine with two grips for pulling a test sample.

items.ask: Who could you ask about what the product needs to do?
items.text: Discuss requirements with the client or user group, and consult specialists to identify key specification criteria. Specialist internet forums help too, and integrated circuit developers are an example of specialists for electronic products.

image.alt: A technician soldering a circuit board at an electronics workbench.

items.ask: Why look at what's fashionable now, and what was popular in the past?
items.text: Investigating historical and current style influences, fashions and trends gives research that can inform design decisions about style. Market research also looks at trends, alongside competing products, price points and gaps.

image.alt: Chairs from different eras displayed in a row in a museum gallery.

items.ask: What limits might a design have to work within?
items.text: Constraints such as size, environment and method of use, which research should identify. Findings are turned into implications for the design, such as dimensions, user priorities or constraints.

image.alt: Design constraints

items.ask: What safety rules might a product and its materials have to meet?
items.text: Check relevant British Standards, and check materials and components are safe and COSHH compliant. British Standards, published by the BSI, can set safety requirements, dimensions and test methods. COSHH covers substances that may harm health.

image.alt: Nine red-bordered hazard pictograms, including flammable, toxic, corrosive and explosive.

items.ask: How do you make sure a product fits the people who use it?
items.text: Analyse anthropometric data so the product is the correct fit for its users. Anthropometric data is the measurement of human body dimensions. Percentiles show where a measurement sits in a population, and the right one to use depends on the product's function.

image.alt: Diagram of a standing person with measurement lines for height, arm span and shoulder width, and a hand grip.

check.q: Give two examples of materials technical information.
Why does a designer analyse anthropometric data?
check.a: To make sure the product is the correct fit for its users.

chunks.label: Inspiration materials
chunks.summary: Collections of images and samples that explore a style and direction.

items.ask: How could you show the look and feel you're aiming for before you design?
items.text: Make a mood board to show the look you're aiming for. A mood board is a collage of relevant images, chosen for suitable styles and colours. It can also help explore form and emotional direction.

image.alt: A collage of landscape photos with fanned-out paint colour swatches on top.

items.ask: How could you collect real colours and materials to work from?
items.text: Collect real samples in an inspiration box. An inspiration box is a box of swatches, colour samples, materials and products. Real samples help you explore texture as well as colour.

items.ask: What makes inspiration materials useful, not just decoration?
items.text: They should lead to design decisions, not become decorative pages with no link to the design proposal. They help explore colour, texture, form, style and emotional direction.

check.a: A collage of relevant images, including suitable styles and colours.

check.q: What does an inspiration box contain?
check.a: Swatches, colour samples, materials and products.

chunks.label: Design specification
chunks.summary: The key criteria the design must meet, written after research.

items.ask: How will you know at the end whether your design is a success?
items.text: By judging it against the design specification, which turns research into criteria. A design specification is a list of the key criteria to address when designing.

image.alt: Design specification

items.ask: When should the specification be written, and why then?
items.text: After the investigation and analysis of research, because it turns those findings into criteria. In the design cycle it comes after investigation and before ideas generation.

items.ask: Are all of a product's requirements equally important?
items.text: Essential requirements matter more than desirable features, and a specification lists both.

image.alt: Essential and desirable

items.ask: In industry, who mainly decides what goes in a specification?
items.text: The client mainly decides what goes in a commercial specification.

items.ask: What makes a specification point easy to check later?
items.text: Making it measurable or testable, so the design can later be judged against it. Strong criteria also explain why they matter.

items.ask: What headings could a specification cover?
items.text: Function, user, environment, sustainability, maintenance, size, weight, ergonomics, aesthetics, cost, quality, safety.

items.ask: Should the specification only be used at the very end?
items.text: It should be referred to all through the design process, not only used as a final evaluation checklist. Evaluation compares evidence against its criteria and identifies the next development action.

check.q: When is a design specification written?
check.a: After investigation and analysis of research.
Any four: function, user, environment, sustainability, maintenance, size, weight, ergonomics, aesthetics, cost, quality, safety.

chunks.label: Ideas generation
chunks.summary: Techniques for creating, rethinking and developing ideas, alone or in teams.

items.ask: How could you lay out everything about a problem on one page to spark ideas?
items.text: Make a mind map. A mind map is a way of setting out the relevant elements visually, to encourage creativity.

image.alt: A colourful mind map with a central topic and branches of linked words.

items.ask: How could you rethink an existing design, one prompt at a time?
items.text: Use SCAMPER: substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, reverse. SCAMPER is a technique for creating new ideas from elements of existing designs. Eliminate means simplifying the design by removing unnecessary elements.

image.alt: SCAMPER

items.ask: Why might a team come up with a better product than one designer alone?
items.text: Pooling members' specialist expertise improves creativity and often gives better products than a single designer. Working together also lowers the risk of finding manufacturing or cost problems very late.

image.alt: A design team at a workshop table with sketches, a laptop and blue prototype parts.

items.ask: How can a design team share ideas when its members are in different places?
items.text: Video conferencing lets them hold creative discussions, just as they would in a meeting. Digital prototypes can also be reviewed by teams in different places.

image.alt: People in a meeting room watching a video call projected on a large screen.

items.ask: How could passing one sheet round a group produce several developed ideas?
items.text: One person draws an idea in the centre, then others develop it further in four boxes around it. The 4x4 technique is a collaborative activity that turns one idea into four development drawings. It brings in a range of alternative ideas and viewpoints.

image.alt: Diagram of a sheet with a lamp idea in the centre and four developed lamp designs in boxes around it.

items.ask: How could a group make sure an idea is looked at from every point of view?
items.text: Use Thinking Hats: six coloured hats are worn in turn, each standing for a different viewpoint. Thinking Hats is a technique, devised by Edward de Bono, for improving creative discussion and collaborative work.

image.alt: Six hats in a row on a workbench: blue, white, red, yellow, green and black.

items.ask: How could feedback from real people shape your early ideas?
items.text: Discuss sketches or models of initial ideas with the client or target market, then use their feedback to modify the design.

image.alt: A designer showing a client folded card models on a workbench.

check.q: What does SCAMPER help a designer do?
check.a: Create new ideas from elements of existing designs.

check.q: How does Edward de Bono's Thinking Hats technique work?
check.a: Six coloured hats are worn in turn, each representing a different viewpoint, to improve creative discussion.

apply.q: A tool company wants to know why its cordless drill is awkward to hold, and how it's made.
tools: Use it and take it apart
reasons: Using and disassembling it gives first-hand knowledge of its ergonomics, components and manufacture
A collage of styles and colours sets the look of the new drill
Prompts such as substitute and eliminate create new ideas
Swatches and samples show suitable colours and materials

apply.q: A furniture company wants new ideas for its best-selling garden chair, building on what works.
reasons: It creates new ideas from elements of an existing design, such as substituting a material
It gathers objective views from other people
It makes sure the product meets the relevant standards
It makes sure the chair is the correct fit

order.q: Put the stages of the design cycle in order, starting from the problem.

quiz.q: Why is the design process usually cyclic rather than linear?
options: Ongoing improvements are important to commercial success
It means no specification is needed
Each stage only has to be done once
It removes the need for testing
quiz.why: The stages repeat as the design is improved, which matters to commercial success.

quiz.q: Every project should go through each stage of the design process in the same depth.
quiz.why: The process gives structure, but projects need different depths of investigation, modelling and testing.

quiz.q: In the design cycle, which stage comes straight after investigation?
quiz.why: Research is investigated and analysed, then the specification is written from it.

quiz.q: Which stage comes last, before the design cycle goes round again?
quiz.why: The prototype is tested and evaluated, and the findings feed the next round.

quiz.q: What does a design brief outline?
options: The needs and wants of a specific user or target market
Measurable criteria for judging the final design
The timings of each manufacturing stage
The results of testing the prototype
quiz.why: The brief sets out the problem and who it is for; the specification comes later.

quiz.q: A design brief can say where existing products are inadequate or unsuitable.
quiz.why: Shortcomings of existing products help show the problem or need.

quiz.q: Why would a designer take apart an existing product?
options: To assess its function, components, materials and manufacture
To set the price of the new product
quiz.why: Disassembly is primary research into how the product works and is made.

quiz.q: Using a product for its intended task gives the designer first-hand knowledge of it.
quiz.why: It is part of primary research into existing products.

quiz.q: Which two methods seek objective views of a product from other people?
quiz.why: Both gather other people's views rather than the designer's own.

quiz.q: Which are examples of materials technical information?
quiz.why: Designers get technical data on materials from specialist researchers.

quiz.q: Why does a designer analyse anthropometric data?
options: To make sure the product is the correct fit for its users
To check materials are safe to handle
quiz.why: Anthropometric data is body measurements, used to get the right fit.

quiz.q: COSHH is about substances that may harm health.
quiz.why: Designers check that materials and components are safe and COSHH compliant.

quiz.q: Size, environment and method of use are examples of what?
quiz.why: Constraints are limits the design has to work within.

quiz.q: What is an inspiration box?
options: A box of swatches, colour samples, materials and products
A collage of images in suitable styles and colours
quiz.why: A mood board is the collage; an inspiration box holds real samples.

quiz.q: Mood boards are decoration and shouldn't affect design decisions.
quiz.why: Inspiration materials should lead to design decisions.

quiz.q: When is a design specification written?
options: After investigation and analysis of research
quiz.why: The specification turns research into criteria for the design.

quiz.q: A specification lists essential requirements, but never desirable features.
quiz.why: It lists essential requirements as well as desirable features.

quiz.q: Who mainly determines a commercial specification?
quiz.why: In commercial design, the client mainly sets the specification.

quiz.q: The specification should be referred to throughout the design process, not just used as a final checklist.
quiz.why: Designers keep checking ideas against it all the way through.

quiz.q: In SCAMPER, what does 'Eliminate' mean?
options: Simplify the design by removing unnecessary elements
Reorganise the design in a radical way
quiz.why: Eliminate simplifies; Reverse reorganises; Adapt borrows; Substitute swaps elements.

quiz.q: In SCAMPER, what does the R stand for?
quiz.why: Reverse: reorganise the design in a radical way.

quiz.q: What is Edward de Bono's Thinking Hats technique?
options: Six coloured hats worn in turn, each a different viewpoint
Four people developing one idea on a sheet
A collage of images and colours
Seven prompts for rethinking a design
quiz.why: It improves creative discussion of ideas and collaborative work.

quiz.q: Collaborative team designing often results in better products than one designer working alone.
quiz.why: It makes the most of specialist expertise to improve creativity.

quiz.q: In the 4x4 technique, what happens after one person draws an idea in the centre of the sheet?
options: Others develop it further in turn, giving four development drawings
Six people each judge it from a different viewpoint
It is compared against the specification
It is made into a card model
quiz.why: It benefits from a range of alternative ideas and viewpoints.

written.q: A company is about to design a new lunchbox for primary school children. Describe what its design brief should contain.
points: A description of the problem or need: the situation the lunchbox must deal with.
Images and details of the context or situation.
Where existing lunchboxes are inadequate or unsuitable.
Information about the client or user group: the children and parents.
A basic description of the product and its key functions.
The key areas to focus on for the product to succeed.
written.model: The brief should describe the problem or need the lunchbox has to meet, with images and details of the situation it will be used in. It should say where existing lunchboxes are inadequate or unsuitable, and give information about the user group, the children and their parents. It should also give a basic description of the lunchbox and its key functions, and the key areas to focus on for it to succeed.
written.note: 1 mark per content point described, up to 4.

written.q: Explain why the design process used in commercial product development is usually cyclic rather than linear.
points: Ongoing improvements are important to commercial success.
So stages such as investigation, modelling and testing are repeated as the design is improved.
written.model: Ongoing improvements are important to a product's commercial success, so instead of going through the stages once, the designers repeat stages such as investigation, modelling and testing as the design is improved.
written.note: 1 mark for the reason, 1 for how it links to repeating the stages.

written.q: Compare a mood board and an inspiration box as inspiration materials.
points: Both organise inspiration and help explore colour, form and style.
Both should lead to design decisions, not just decoration.
A mood board is a collage of relevant images.
It shows appropriate styles and colours.
An inspiration box holds real swatches, colour samples, materials and products.
So it lets the designer explore real materials and textures, not just pictures.
written.model: Both are ways of organising inspiration to explore colour, form and style, and both should lead to design decisions rather than being decoration. A mood board is a collage of relevant images showing appropriate styles and colours, whereas an inspiration box holds real swatches, colour samples, materials and products, so the designer can explore real materials and textures rather than pictures.
written.note: 1 mark per valid point, up to 4. At least one similarity and one difference for full marks.

written.q: Explain why a designer would analyse existing products as part of their primary research.
points: To find their strengths, weaknesses and areas for improvement.
Using a product for its intended task gives first-hand knowledge of it.
Taking it apart shows its function, components, materials and manufacture.
Comparing these with equivalent products shows which works best.
Assessing ergonomics, aesthetics and cost shows whether it meets consumer needs.
written.model: Analysing existing products shows their strengths, weaknesses and areas for improvement, which the new design can build on. Using a product for its intended task gives the designer first-hand knowledge of it, and taking it apart shows its function, components, materials and manufacture. Comparing these with equivalent products, and assessing ergonomics, aesthetics and cost, shows whether consumer needs are met.
written.note: 1 mark per point explained, up to 4.

written.q: Describe two ideas generation methods that a design team could use.
points: SCAMPER: new ideas from existing designs by substituting, combining, adapting, modifying, putting to another use, eliminating or reversing.
Mind map: sets out the relevant elements visually to encourage creativity.
4x4 technique: one person draws an idea in the centre; others develop it in turn into four drawings.
Thinking Hats: six coloured hats worn in turn, each a different viewpoint, to improve creative discussion.
Collaborative team designing: makes the most of specialist expertise, through meetings or video conferencing.
Discussion: designs are discussed with the client or target market, and feedback is used to modify them.
written.model: In the 4x4 technique, one person draws an idea in the centre of a sheet, then others develop it in turn, giving four development drawings around it from different viewpoints. In Edward de Bono's Thinking Hats, six coloured hats are worn in turn, each standing for a different viewpoint, which improves the creative discussion of ideas.
written.note: Up to 2 marks per method: 1 for naming it, 1 for describing how it works.

written.q: Evaluate the importance of the design specification in the design process.
points: It is written after investigation and analysis, so it is based on research.
It lists essential requirements and desirable features, so priorities are clear.
Commercial specifications are mainly set by the client, so the design meets the client's needs.
It covers elements such as function, user, cost, quality and safety.
It is referred to throughout the process, not only as a final checklist.
Criteria need to be measurable or testable; vague ones are hard to judge the design against.
Justified conclusion, e.g. it is central to the process, as long as its criteria are based on research and can be tested.
written.model: The specification is written after investigation and analysis, so it turns research into the key criteria the design must meet. It lists essential requirements as well as desirable features, and in commercial design it is mainly set by the client, so the design keeps to the client's needs. It covers elements such as function, user, cost, quality and safety, and it is referred to throughout the process, not only as a final checklist. However, it is only useful if its criteria are measurable or testable: a vague criterion is hard to judge a design against. So the specification is central to the design process, as long as it is based on research and its criteria can be tested.
written.note: Tick the points made, then use the levels under the model answer to decide the mark.

levels.text: Detailed, balanced points on both sides, with a justified conclusion.
Some points, mostly on one side, or a conclusion that isn't justified.
